International Stroke Trial: sorted-effects pilot

Aspirin, six-month death or dependence, and validation of effect rankings

Published

October 22, 2026

International Stroke Trial: what does the first check show?

The interaction model gives a wider spread of fitted benefits, but its ranking is not convincingly supported by held-out outcomes. A common-odds-ratio model already produces variation in absolute benefit through baseline risk. These are useful teaching results, with no claim of a newly established treatment subgroup.

This is an exploratory reanalysis of public trial data. The model specifications, outcome, classification characteristics and one validation split were written down before fitting the heterogeneity models. The unadjusted arm risks had already been inspected. Analysis plan · Data preparation and source · Analysis code · Validation code

Data and treatment contrast

The International Stroke Trial randomized 19,435 patients to aspirin or no aspirin, alongside randomized heparin allocation. We compare randomized aspirin allocation, averaging over that heparin allocation. The endpoint is death or dependence at six months, using the corrected dataset’s derived OCCODE.

Arm Randomized Outcome observed Outcome missing Death or dependence (%)
No aspirin 9715 9646 69 63.50
Aspirin 9720 9639 81 62.25

The unadjusted difference among observed outcomes is 1.25 percentage points in favor of aspirin. Missing outcomes affect 150 patients (0.77%). Assigning all missing outcomes in either direction gives an average-risk-difference range of 0.49 to 2.03 percentage points. That range describes missing-outcome sensitivity; it is not a sampling confidence interval.

Age, sex, blood pressure and randomization delay are complete. Clinical unknowns and unassessable deficits have explicit categories. There are no smoking or alcohol measurements. Only baseline characteristics enter the effect models.

Two models, the same average effect

Both models include age, sex, age-by-sex, blood pressure, delay, consciousness, atrial fibrillation, prior aspirin, neurological deficits and stroke subtype. Age, blood pressure and delay use natural splines. One model has a common aspirin odds ratio. The other adds eight specified aspirin interactions with baseline characteristics, including age-by-sex.

Model Parameters Average reduction (pp) 10th percentile (pp) 90th percentile (pp)
Constant odds ratio 28 1.31 0.42 1.83
Treatment interactions 36 1.31 -0.93 4.07

The interaction-model average reduction is 1.31 pp, with a native 95% bootstrap interval of 0.17 to 2.46 pp. The joint test of the eight added interactions gives p = 0.35. This tests added interactions on the log-odds scale, rather than constancy of risk differences.

  • The two models estimate almost the same average benefit.
  • Adding interactions widens the fitted distribution, including negative estimates for some profiles. These do not establish that aspirin harms those patients.
  • A common odds ratio also produces a sloping SPE curve: absolute benefits vary with baseline risk.
  • Shading shows the original package’s 95% uniform band over the displayed grid, separately for each model. It is not a joint band over both models.

The primary regressions average over randomized heparin allocation through the observed data. A sensitivity analysis explicitly includes heparin allocation and averages predicted risks over its allocation proportions. The average absolute change in individual profile predictions is 0.00 pp for the interaction model; its ranking correlation with the primary specification is 1.000.

A larger classification table

These are characteristics of the bottom and top 10% of fitted risk reductions from the interaction model. Each tail contains 1929 patients. They are formed using predicted effects across both randomized arms.

Characteristic Bottom 10% Top 10% Top minus bottom Bootstrap SE Joint p
Age (years) 71.4 71.2 -0.2 10.0 1.00
Female (%) 61.9 30.5 -31.4 42.5 0.99
Systolic BP (mmHg) 134.3 188.0 53.8 19.0 0.16
Delay to randomization (hours) 23.7 16.8 -6.9 11.6 1.00
Atrial fibrillation recorded (%) 1.2 28.0 26.8 24.4 0.95
Atrial fibrillation unknown (%) 5.7 4.4 -1.3 2.0 1.00
Prior aspirin recorded (%) 16.0 22.2 6.2 4.0 0.74
Drowsy or unconscious (%) 61.4 0.7 -60.7 35.2 0.64
Leg deficit recorded (%) 97.4 21.7 -75.7 34.7 0.34
Dysphasia recorded (%) 43.5 45.9 2.4 10.2 1.00
Men aged 75 or older (%) 7.2 29.8 22.6 23.8 0.97
Women younger than 65 (%) 5.9 9.7 3.8 19.8 1.00

Percentage-row differences and SEs are in percentage points. “Recorded” means documented present; its complement can include unknown measurements. AF unknown also identifies the pilot participants with unrecorded previous-aspirin status.

Joint p-values adjust across these 12 specified characteristics. They test differences in the selected tails’ mean characteristics. They do not test that a characteristic modifies treatment effects or that a treatment rule works. The bootstrap re-estimates the model, tail thresholds and tail means. The package does not return native confidence intervals for these moment differences. A Monte Carlo zero is displayed as p < .01, not as an exactly zero probability.

Some descriptive gaps are large: mean systolic pressure is 134 versus 188 mmHg in the two tails. After refitting and reclassification, however, none of these 12 comparisons has a joint p-value below .05; the smallest is 0.16. Large differences in the fitted table do not by themselves establish stable treatment-benefit profiles.

The connecting lines are descriptive differences, not confidence intervals. The two joint demographic rows make combinations such as older men visible; they overlap with the ordinary age and sex rows.

Does the ranking work in held-out patients?

One fixed, treatment-stratified split uses 9,642 training patients and 9,643 validation patients. Both models are fitted using training outcomes only. Validation patients are then grouped using frozen predicted benefits.

The interaction model predicts a top-versus-bottom quintile difference of 7.36 pp. In validation data, the observed difference is 0.41 pp (95% interval -5.73 to 6.55 pp). The wide interval includes zero, and the predicted ordering is not reproduced consistently.

Model Validation slope 95% interval Raw p (slope = 0) Holm p (two rankings)
Constant odds ratio 3.56 0.30 to 6.81 0.032 0.064
Treatment interactions 0.08 -0.60 to 0.76 0.822 0.822

The slope uses a benefit pseudo-outcome based on randomized assignment and training-only outcome predictions, with HC3 standard errors. A positive slope indicates agreement between the predicted ranking and validation outcomes; a slope of one corresponds to linear calibration. The common-odds-ratio ranking has a suggestive signal, but its quintile pattern is irregular and its adjusted p-value exceeds .05. This does not establish a validated treatment rule.

The five plotted group intervals are pointwise and unadjusted. Holm adjustment covers the two ranking slopes only; it does not account for every reported diagnostic. This is one internal split, not external replication.

What this could add to the journal club

The trial gives a concrete example of why three questions need separate answers:

  1. Does the average treatment effect favor aspirin? The average estimated reduction is around one percentage point.
  2. Do fitted absolute effects vary? Yes, even under a common odds ratio.
  3. Do added interactions give a useful, reproducible ranking? This first check does not provide convincing support.

The classification table adds clinical detail, while validation limits how far we can interpret it. A reasonable presentation would show the tempting fitted pattern and then its uncertainty and held-out performance. A claim that a subgroup finding is new would also require a focused literature review.

Reproduce and inspect

Secondary check: ACTG 175

A fixed secondary analysis compares zidovudine plus didanosine with zidovudine alone in 1,054 participants, using 20-week CD4 count. This provides a continuous outcome and eight baseline characteristics. Both models estimate about 71 additional CD4 cells/mm³, with an interaction-model 95% interval of about 58 to 84. The joint eight-interaction test gives p = .230; the held-out ranking slope gives p = .423. That pilot also produces fitted variation without convincing validation of the added interaction ranking.

No additional arms, outcomes or validation splits were searched. The public export’s selection relative to the original trial cohort has not been verified. ACTG 175 plan, findings and classification table · ACTG 175 analysis code

Run the IST analysis

source /workspace/.tools/activate
python3 scripts/fetch-ist-data.py --verify-only
Rscript scripts/analyze-ist.R
Rscript scripts/validate-ist-ranking.R
Rscript scripts/plot-ist.R
quarto render ist-pilot.qmd --to html

The primary inference uses SortedEffects 1.7.0, 499 bootstrap draws, seed 420, uncorrected estimates and the 10th–90th percentile grid. Native point estimates are checked against direct model contrasts. The full-sample SPE band holds original profiles and quantile weights fixed; CA uses its reweighted moment bootstrap. The outcome model and patient bootstrap are working assumptions. They do not establish robustness to misspecification, hospital clustering or the trial’s exact allocation algorithm. The complete-outcome analysis also requires assumptions about the missing endpoints.
